In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

74 % and 26 % of all recorded lesions in this study were less frequent in organic/free-range and conventional pigs, respectively, and that the remaining 5 % of all the recorded lesions did not differ between the two production systems.

5 out of 13 lesions types are more frequent in organic/free-range than in conventional indoor finishers, but these five lesion types represent 74 %, 73 %, and 75 % of the lesions recorded among organic/free-range, conventional free-range, and conventional indoor finishers respectively.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

13 lesions are more prevalent in organic/free-range compared to conventional pigs, and that 74 % (5) of all lesions occur less frequently among organic/free-range finisher pigs compared to conventional indoor pigs.
5 of the 13 lesion types recorded in the study by Alban et al., 2015, are the most frequent and that they occur more often in conventional pigs than in organic pigs.

there is no evidence that organic/free-range production forms have a higher risk of having lesions at the time of meat inspection compared to conventional indoor finishers, but that the risk of having lesions is higher in conventional free-range compared to conventional indoor pigs.

the prevalence of 5 lesion types (pneumonic lesions, pericardial effusion, pericarditis, pleuritis and abscesses) are lower in organic/free-range compared to conventional indoor finishers, and the prevalence of these lesion types is higher in conventional free-range compared to conventional finisher.
